list_states consumers outside MCP dir: reads_cli.py:344 (list CLI arm), validate.py:67 (_raw_tickets -> reads.list_states), next_batch.py:144 (_reads.list_states)

findings.finding: AC-2 is contradictory about the edit locus of the field-drop, leaving out-of-dir consumers of list_states unenumerated. It both (a) says the shared lean_projection is 'called by BOTH backends: list_states and _snapshot/ticket_view.py::TicketView.list_by_query' — which implies editing list_states/TicketView.list_by_query themselves — and (b) says the projection 'happens one layer up, in the MCP tool (_mcp_reads._discovery_rows)' and 'The LIBRARY is left alone.' If (a), list_states' non-MCP consumers — reads_cli.py:344 (the CLI `list` arm), validate._raw_tickets (validate.py:67 -> reads.list_states), and next_batch.py:144 (_reads.list_states) — would newly lose authorship_ledger/attestations/signature/keyring, yet the plan only reasons about the description/comments bodies for these internal callers, never these four signature fields.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria, AC-2 (One shared lean projection)
scenarios: If lean_projection is edited into list_states, the CLI `list` output and validate/next_batch inputs silently lose authorship_ledger/attestations/signature/keyring
A reviewer/implementer cannot tell whether list_states is an edit target or merely the list_tickets path that _discovery_rows sits above
findings.suggested_fix: Apply lean_projection ONLY in the MCP _discovery_rows helper (over rows already returned by list_tickets/ready), leaving list_states and TicketView.list_by_query byte-identical, and reword AC-2 to say the shared function is CALLED FROM the MCP tool rather than 'called by BOTH backends'; if instead the backends must be edited, add an explicit line enumerating that reads_cli.py:344, validate.py:67, and next_batch.py:144 do not consume the four dropped fields (or are given full=True).

findings.checklist_item: State the code-level rollback path (how to revert the deployed bound quickly without data cleanup) and confirm whether ready_tickets' ~1.7% headroom risks an all-traffic refusal that a staged rollout or a temporarily-higher/disable-able budget would de-risk.
evidence: 'Both halves reach all deployed traffic at once. That is accepted because the refusal is ADDITIVE ... and the narrowing is reversible per-call via full=True'
ready_tickets 'measured headroom is ~1.7%' — a small change in the store could push default ready_tickets over budget and refuse for every caller at once
T12 checklist: 'An explicit, cheap, tested way to undo quickly' — the plan names per-call full=True but no code-level rollback path
findings.finding: The plan ships both the payload bound and the default-output narrowing to 100% of deployed traffic in a single flip; the only reversibility offered is per-call (full=True), which each individual caller must opt into after they are already affected. There is no staged rollout/canary and no described way to roll back the deployed code itself if the bound misfires (e.g. refuses a legitimately-needed under-headroom ready_tickets call whose measured headroom is only ~1.7%).
findings.location: AC 'Rollout. Both halves reach all deployed traffic at once.'
scenarios: A store growth pushes default ready_tickets (1.7% headroom) over 90,000 bytes; every ready_tickets caller now gets a refusal simultaneously with no canary having caught it, and the only recovery is re-deploying since full=True still returns the same over-budget rows.

findings.checklist_item: For ready_tickets' refusal remedy, establish that next_batch(epic_id) (or another named tool) actually reconstructs the refused global ready set — e.g. specify enumerating epics then next_batch per epic, or add a paging/narrowing argument to ready_tickets — so the remedy is executable and result-equivalent, not merely a different tool name.
evidence: Plan: "ready_tickets' refusal points at next_batch(epic_id) instead. Its measured headroom is ~1.7% ... so refusing is a near-term state and the remedy has to work."
Code: ready_tickets(sort) returns rebar.ready(sort=sort) — a global ready set; next_batch(epic_id) returns NextBatchOut scoped to one epic's hierarchy, not equivalent coverage.
next_batch requires a mandatory epic_id argument (def next_batch(epic_id)), so there is no zero-argument path to the global ready set.
findings.finding: For ready_tickets, the sole offered remedy (next_batch(epic_id)) returns unblocked tickets under ONE epic's hierarchy, which is not result-equivalent to the global 'all ready tickets' query being refused; with ~1.7% headroom the tool refuses near-term, so the remedy must be a workable path to the same information, but the plan does not establish one (e.g. it names next_batch without showing how a caller reconstructs the full ready set from per-epic batches).
findings.location: AC: 'The remedy must be one the REFUSED TOOL can execute.'
scenarios: A store where ready_tickets exceeds the 90,000-byte budget: caller is refused and told to use next_batch, but has no epic_id in hand and no way to enumerate the same tickets globally.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State whether the byte measurement can short-circuit (e.g. incremental/streaming byte accumulation or an early row-count/size cutoff) so the guard does not have to fully serialize a multi-megabyte payload before refusing.
evidence: 'the bound runs INSIDE the tool body after TicketStateOut.model_validate and CALLS js_safe_result on those rows itself'
Root cause: unfiltered payload is '94,541,551 bytes over 177.29 seconds'
findings.finding: The bound is measured by calling js_safe_result on the fully-validated rows INSIDE the tool body, which materializes and serializes the entire oversized payload (up to the measured 94.5 MB) before it can refuse — the guard pays the full serialization cost of the very payload it exists to reject.
findings.location: AC: 'Bounded, measured at a named seam.'
scenarios: A store whose lean payload is far over budget still forces a full serialize-then-measure pass before the structured refusal is raised
